newsitem.title: UK: Mutations give extra boost to bugs, studies find.
newsitem.headline: Mutations give extra boost to bugs, studies find.

text.p: Bacteria and viruses can give an extra boost to their mutation rates, which could explain how drug-resistant forms can emerge so fast, scientists reported on Wednesday.
Two reports in the science journal Nature described how microbes can sometimes turbo-charge their mutation rate, helping them evolve to survive in a changing environment.
Most mutations harm, not help, so the natural mutation rate is usually low.
But Paul Sniegowski of the University of Pennsylvania and colleagues at Michigan State University and Francois Taddei and colleagues at the University of Paris said sometimes microbes break the rule.
Every once in a while a new type of bacteria, called a "mutator", arises -- and it can make copies of itself even more quickly than usual, they said.
More study is needed to see if the mutator strains are more successful than normal varieties, they added.
Sniegowski's group made 12 cloned populations of E coli bacteria -- a common gut bacteria that occasionally develops into a strain that can cause deadly food poisoning.
They were all genetically identical, so the only possible variations would arise through genetic mutation.
They were put into an unusual environment -- low on the sugars E coli thrives on -- which was meant to encourage adaptive evolution.

"Most of the populations retained the ancestral mutation rate, but three populations displayed mutation rates that were between one and two orders of magnitude higher than those in the ancestor," they wrote.
"Our results...may help to explain observations that associate high mutation rates with emerging pathogens and with certain cancers."
David Thaler, a geneticist at Rockefeller University in New York, said research had indicated such mutator strains existed in E coli and salmonella, another bacteria that can cause food poisoning.
Thaler said in a telephone interview that when drug cocktails are thrown at infection such as tuberculosis, the few bacteria that do survive tend to be the mutator ones.
"It's something to worry about," he said. "I think what is really dawning on people is that mutation rate...is an inherited genetic property."
The next step would be to see if indeed the mutators were "We don't have proof that this is really part of the disease process. We're hinting at it," he said.
